title: Things We Believed Before the Scientific Method
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck explore pre-scientific-method beliefs that were long accepted despite being wrong. They cover the Four Humors of medicine (Hippocrates, Galen, bloodletting and balance of humors), Eudoxus's geocentric shell model and its five assumptions, the Pythagorean central fire and counter-earth, the four classical elements (Empedocles, Aristotle, Plato) and the atomic theory of Democritus, which was vindicated later by Torricelli's vacuum experiment. The final topic is spontaneous generation: von Helmont's recipes, Redi's maggot experiment, microscopy, Pasteur's sterilization work, and the rival theories of epigenesis and preformationism. The episode closes with listener mail about the use of "a" versus "an" before "historic" and a request for a pro wrestling episode.

segments.title: Opening and overview of pre-scientific beliefs
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on beliefs held before the scientific method and explain how the scientific method tests hypotheses while earlier thinkers relied on observation and philosophy.

segments.title: Four Humors and humoral medicine
segments.summary: Humoral medicine from Hippocrates and Galen held that blood, yellow bile, black bile and phlegm governed health, with hot/cold and wet/dry qualities; treatments aimed to restore balance, such as bloodletting. Harvey's demonstration of the heart's pumping later undermined it, and Ayurveda shares similar ideas.

segments.title: Eudoxus and geocentric shell model
segments.summary: Eudoxus of Cnidus's five assumptions about celestial motion, including an Earth-centered universe with circular, regular motion, and the earlier idea of celestial shells attributed to Anaximenes. Kepler later showed orbits are elliptical.

segments.title: Pythagorean central fire and counter earth
segments.summary: Philolaus and the Pythagoreans proposed that the Earth, Sun, Moon, planets and an unseen counter earth orbit a central fire in circular orbits, totaling ten, with ten considered perfect. The hosts note the counter earth was later ruled out by modeling.

segments.title: Four elements: earth, air, fire, water
segments.summary: The four-element theory, linked to Anaximenes, Plato, and Aristotle (who added ether). Observations such as wood being solid, floating and burning were used to support it. Empedocles proposed elements combined by attractive forces he called love.

segments.title: Empedocles, Democritus and early atomic theory
segments.summary: Democritus proposed indivisible, indestructible atoms moving in void, a remarkably accurate guess, though he thought each substance had its own kind of atom. Aristotle rejected the void and sided with the four elements.

segments.title: Torricelli's vacuum and vindication of atomic theory
segments.summary: Torricelli created an experimental vacuum in 1643, showing air has weight and vindicating Democritus's idea of a void; this led to the barometer and later investigation into atomic theory, put forth by John Dalton around 1803.

segments.title: Spontaneous generation, Pasteur and rival theories of reproduction
segments.summary: Spontaneous generation was a long-held belief; van Helmont claimed mice from grain and scorpions from basil, and Redi showed maggots did not arise from meat when flies were kept off. Microscopes revealed microbes, and Pasteur's sterilization work helped end the idea. Epigenesis and preformationism were rival theories of reproduction.

segments.title: Listener mail: a versus an before historic and pro wrestling request
segments.summary: A listener's email about using 'an' versus 'a' before words starting with H, with examples such as 'an historic'. The hosts discuss the rule and mention a listener request for a pro wrestling episode.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts invite listener requests by email and close the episode.
